hints: Different moves measure different kinds of disorder.
Cycles describe arbitrary swaps; increasing subsequences describe moving elements anywhere.
For moves only to the front, keep the longest final consecutive suffix already in order.
analogy: Each operation has its own measure of what can stay untouched.
example: For [2,1,3], one adjacent swap, one arbitrary swap, one move anywhere, or moving 1 to the front each sorts the array.
algorithm: Count inversions using a Fenwick tree for adjacent swaps. Decompose the permutation into cycles and sum cycle length minus one for arbitrary swaps. Compute n minus the length of a longest increasing subsequence for moves to arbitrary positions. For moves to the front, scan from right to left looking for n,n-1,...; if t consecutive largest values are found in that order, output n-t. Print the four values in the requested order.
correctness: An adjacent swap changes inversion count by at most one, and bubble sorting achieves it. A cycle of length L needs L-1 arbitrary swaps. Elements never moved by the third method must form an increasing subsequence, and an LIS can stay. For front moves, untouched values must form the increasing suffix k,k+1,...,n; keeping the longest such suffix and moving the rest in descending value order is optimal.
complexity: For n elements, inversion counting and LIS take O(n log n) time; all other steps take O(n). Space is O(n).
